currencyTrapAnswers.answer:
Yes — under the passages provided, an annual registration fee of ₱500 is due for every separate or distinct establishment or place of business (including facility types where sales transactions occur), payable upon registration and every year thereafter on or before the last day of January [1].

Exceptions and details:
- Not liable: cooperatives, individuals earning purely compensation income (local or abroad), and overseas workers [1].
- Pay it to an authorized agent bank in your revenue district, or to the Revenue Collection Officer or authorized city/municipal Treasurer where each place of business or branch is registered [1].
- If you voluntarily register for VAT as an exempt person, you also pay this annual fee [5].

As a self-employed professional with a registered business, the fee applies. This is general guidance, not professional tax advice.

supersededBy.change: annual registration fee under Section 236(B) abolished

currencyTrapAnswers.answer:
Yes. All persons subject to internal revenue tax must issue duly registered receipts or sales/commercial invoices at the point of each sale or service rendered valued at ₱100 or more, showing date, quantity, unit cost and nature of service [8]. Where the receipt covers payment of rentals, commissions, compensation or **fees** (like professional fees), it must also show the name, business style (if any), and address of the purchaser/client [8]. If your client is VAT-registered, the receipt must also show the client's TIN [6][8].

Other points:
- You must first secure a BIR authority to print, and receipts must be serially numbered and bear your name, business style, TIN and business address [1].
- Give the original to the client; keep the duplicate at your place of business for 3 years from the close of the taxable year of issuance (digital records for e-receipts) [6].
- The Commissioner may exempt persons in meritorious cases [6].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

supersededBy.change: invoices replace official receipts as the primary document for sales of services under Section 237

currencyTrapAnswers.answer:
For 2023, the PhilHealth premium rate for direct contributors was **4.50%**, with a monthly income floor of ₱10,000.00 and an income ceiling of ₱90,000.00 [1].

Note that failure to pay premiums does not bar enjoyment of benefits, but self-employed direct contributors must pay all missed contributions with compounded interest [3].

This is general guidance, not professional tax advice.

rows.answer:
Yes. A self-employed individual/professional whose gross sales/receipts and other non-operating income does not exceed the VAT threshold (₱3,000,000) may opt for an 8% tax on gross sales/receipts and other non-operating income in excess of ₱250,000, in lieu of the graduated rates under Sec. 24(A)(2)(a) and the percentage tax under Sec. 116 [2][4][7].

Conditions:
- You must signify the intention to elect 8% in the 1st Quarter Percentage and/or Income Tax Return (or the initial quarter return after starting a new business/profession); otherwise you are deemed to have chosen the graduated rates. The election is irrevocable for that taxable year [2][5].
- Not available if you are VAT-registered, or subject to other percentage taxes under Title V (except Sec. 116), or a GPP partner as to the distributive share [2][5].
- If sales exceed the ₱3M threshold during the year, you automatically fall under graduated rates, with credit for prior quarterly payments [5].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

rows.answer:
You must signify the intention to elect the 8% rate in the **1st Quarter Percentage and/or Income Tax Return**, or on the initial quarter return of the taxable year after commencing a new business/practice of profession [1][3]. If you don't signify it, you are considered to have availed of the graduated rates under Sec. 24(A)(2)(a) [1][3].

No, you cannot change it: the election is **irrevocable** and no amendment of option may be made for that taxable year [1][3].

Related steps if you're an existing non-VAT taxpayer:

- File BIR Form 1905 to end-date the Percentage Tax type before the start of the year or the percentage tax due date [5][7].
- If you can't update in time, keep filing the Percentage Tax return at zero with a notation that you're availing of the 8% option, and still signify the option in the initial quarterly income tax return [5][7].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

If the taxpayer is unable to timely update the required registration, s/he shall continue to file the Percentage Tax return reflecting a zero-amount of tax with a notation that s/he is availing of the 8% Income Tax rate option for the taxable year. S/he is still required to signify the intention to avail the option on the initial Quarterly Income Tax Return for Income Tax purposes. On the other hand, if the non-VAT taxpayer opted to be taxed under the graduated Income Tax rates, s/he shall continue to pay the required Percentage Tax under Sec. 116 of the Tax Code, as amended. A taxpayer who initially presumed that the gross sales/receipts and other non-operating income for the taxable year will not exceed the P 3,000,000.00 VAT threshold but has actually exceeded the same during the taxable year shall immediately update his/her registration to reflect the change in tax profile from non-VAT to a VAT taxpayer. rows.answer:
Effective January 1, 2023 and onwards, the graduated rates on annual taxable income are [1][3][8]:

- Not over ₱250,000 — exempt (0%)
- Over ₱250,000 to ₱400,000 — 15% of excess over ₱250,000
- Over ₱400,000 to ₱800,000 — ₱22,500 + 20% of excess over ₱400,000
- Over ₱800,000 to ₱2,000,000 — ₱102,500 + 25% of excess over ₱800,000
- Over ₱2,000,000 to ₱8,000,000 — ₱402,500 + 30% of excess over ₱2,000,000
- Over ₱8,000,000 — ₱2,202,500 + 35% of excess over ₱8,000,000

For Jan. 1, 2018–Dec. 31, 2022, the brackets were 20%/25%/30%/32%/35% with basic amounts of ₱30,000, ₱130,000, ₱490,000 and ₱2,410,000 [1][8]. Minimum wage earners are exempt from income tax [3]. Self-employed individuals/professionals below the ₱3,000,000 VAT threshold may instead opt for the 8% rate on gross sales/receipts over ₱250,000 [3][7]. General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

rows.answer:
**Section 116 percentage tax = 3% of gross quarterly sales or receipts.** It is paid by any person whose sales/receipts are VAT-exempt under Section 109 and who is **not** VAT-registered [2].

Filing and exceptions:
- The return is filed quarterly, with the tax paid within 25 days after the end of each taxable quarter; if your VAT registration is cancelled and you become liable under Sec. 116, the tax accrues from the date of cancellation [1].
- You are **not** liable for Sec. 116 tax if you validly elect the 8% income tax rate, since the 8% is in lieu of both the graduated rates and the Sec. 116 percentage tax [4][7]. If you instead choose graduated rates, you continue paying the Sec. 116 percentage tax [5][6].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

Individuals engaged in business or practice of profession — regardless of the amount of sales/receipts — must file Quarterly Income Tax Returns on or before **May 15, August 15, and November 15** for the first, second, and third quarters of the current year, plus an annual return by April 15 (the 15th day of the fourth month after the close of the calendar year) [2].

Related points:
- If the annual tax due exceeds P2,000, you may pay in two equal installments: the first upon filing the annual return, the second on or before October 15 [2].
- Missing an installment date makes the whole unpaid tax due immediately, with delinquency penalties reckoned from the original due date [1].

This is general guidance, not professional tax advice.

rows.answer:
A mixed income earner (employment plus business/profession) is taxed as follows:

- **If the 8% option is chosen for business income:** total tax = tax on taxable compensation using the graduated rates + 8% of total gross sales/receipts and other non-operating income from business/profession [1][7]. The 8% is in lieu of the graduated tax and the Section 116 percentage tax on that business income [7].
- **If the graduated rates are chosen:** taxable income from compensation and from business/practice of profession are combined, and the graduated rates are applied to the total [1][7][5]. Percentage tax may still apply (e.g., 3% of gross sales in the illustration) [5].

Key condition: the ₱250,000 deduction allowed to purely self-employed taxpayers does not apply to mixed income earners under the 8% option, since it is already built into the first tier of the graduated rates; any unused portion is not creditable against business income [2][7][8]. The 8% option is also unavailable if gross sales exceed the VAT threshold [2].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

Yes. SSS coverage is compulsory for self-employed persons as determined by the Commission, including all self-employed professionals, partners and single proprietors, actors/directors/scriptwriters/news correspondents not classified as employees, professional athletes/coaches/trainers/jockeys, and individual farmers and fishermen [3]. A self-employed person is treated as both employee and employer at the same time [2][5], and provisions applicable to covered employees generally apply to covered self-employed persons too [3].

Things to note:
- You must register and report to SSS within 30 days from the first day you started practicing your profession or business operations, including your average monthly net income and dependents [8].
- If you realize no income in a given month, you may continue paying contributions as a voluntary member, following the self-employed payment deadlines [1].

This is general guidance, not professional tax advice.

Direct contributors are those who have the capacity to pay premiums, namely: [2]

rows.answer:
Yes. Pag-IBIG coverage is mandatory for a self-employed person, regardless of trade, business or occupation, with an income of at least P1,000 a month and not over 60 years old — including self-employed professionals, single proprietors, business partners, board directors, freelancers not under an employer-employee relationship, farmers/fisherfolk, and informal-sector workers [4]. Coverage is likewise mandatory for all employees compulsorily covered by the SSS [1].

Points to note:
- A self-employed person subject to compulsory SSS coverage is treated by the Fund as both employee and employer, so both the employee and employer shares must be paid [4][2].
- Actual SSS membership is not required; it is enough that the person ought to be compulsorily covered by SSS [4].
- The self-employed subject to compulsory coverage must register with the Fund within 30 days from starting [8].

Under the Pag-IBIG Fund Law and its IRR, contributions are based on the covered employee's monthly compensation [1][2]:

- Employees earning not more than P1,500/month \u2014 1% [1][2]
- Employees earning more than P1,500/month \u2014 2% [1][2]
- All employers \u2014 2% of the monthly compensation of all covered employees [1][2]

The maximum monthly compensation used in computing both employee and employer contributions is P5,000.00, though the Board may adjust this maximum and the rates from time to time [1][2]. The same rates apply to self-employed and voluntary members, and a member may contribute more if desired \u2014 but an employer is only required to match up to the mandated amount unless it agrees otherwise [1]. Employers cannot deduct or recover their own share from employees' compensation [1][2].

This is general guidance, not professional tax advice.

citations.content: RULE VI CONTRIBUTIONS Section 1. Rate of Contributions. Covered employees and employers shall contribute to the Fund based on the monthly compensation of covered employees as follows: a. Employees earning not more than One thousand five hundred pesos (P1,500.00) per month – one percent (1 %). b. Employees earning more than One thousand five hundred pesos (P1,500.00) per month -two percent (2%). c. All employers – two percent (2%) of the monthly compensation of all covered employees. The maximum monthly compensation to be used in computing employee and employer contributions shall not be more than Five thousand pesos (P5,000.00); Provided, that this maximum and the contribution rates may be fixed from time to time by the Board through rules and regulations adopted by it, taking into consideration actuarial calculations and rates of benefits. Provided further, that the foregoing rates shall likewise be the same for the self-employed and voluntary members. A member may, however, be allowed to contribute more than what is required herein should he or she so desires. The employer, however, shall only be mandated to contribute what is required under these Rules unless the employer agrees to match the member’s increased contribution. Notwithstanding any contract to the contrary, an employer shall not deduct, directly or indirectly, from the compensation of its employees covered by the Fund, or otherwise recover from them, the employer’s contribution with respect to such employees. Section 2. Full-time Spouse. Full-time spouses who volunteer to be covered by the Fund as provided for under these Rules, shall adopt as a basis of monthly contributions one-half (½) of the monthly compensation income of the employed spouse. The full-time spouse shall not be required to pay the employer’s contribution. Section 3. Contributions of Member with Multiple Employers. In cases where a member has two or more employers, such member shall contribute monthly to the Fund a percentage of his or her monthly compensation per employer, which shall be matched by the latter in accordance with Section 1 of this Rule. Persons required by law to pay internal revenue taxes must keep a journal and a ledger or their equivalents [4][8]. If quarterly sales, earnings, receipts or output do not exceed P50,000, a simplified set of bookkeeping records authorized by the Secretary of Finance may be used instead, showing all transactions and results of operations so taxes can be readily ascertained [4][1]. Subsidiary books are optional but, if kept, form part of the accounting system and follow the same rules [1].

Other conditions:
- Books must be in a native language, English or Spanish; other-language records need a certified true translation [1][2].

- Books must be preserved from the last entry until the last day of the assessment period under Section 203 [2].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

Under Section 236(A), every person subject to any internal revenue tax must register once with the appropriate Revenue District Officer — on or before the commencement of business (or within 10 days from date of employment) [5]. The registration must state the taxpayer's name, style, place of residence, business, and other information the Commissioner requires, with the Commissioner directed to simplify registration and tax compliance requirements for self-employed individuals and/or professionals [3].

VAT registration is also required if [3]:
- Gross sales/receipts for the past 12 months (excluding those exempt under Sec. 109(A) to (BB)) exceeded ₱3,000,000; or
- There are reasonable grounds to believe such gross sales/receipts for the next 12 months will exceed ₱3,000,000.

Exempt persons may optionally register for VAT, but those who elected the 8% tax on gross sales/receipts cannot avail of this option [3].

This is general guidance, not professional tax advice.

Under Section 51(A)(1), the following must file an income tax return [3]:

- Every Filipino citizen residing in the Philippines
- Every Filipino citizen residing abroad, on Philippine-source income
- Every alien residing in the Philippines, on Philippine-source income
- Every nonresident alien engaged in trade or business or exercising a profession in the Philippines

Exceptions (Sec. 51(A)(2)): an individual whose gross income does not exceed personal/additional exemptions — but a Filipino citizen or alien engaged in business or practice of profession in the Philippines must file regardless of gross income [3]; an individual with pure compensation income correctly withheld under Sec. 79 (though those with two or more employers during the year must file) [3][6]; an individual whose sole income was subjected to final withholding tax; and an individual exempt from income tax [6]. Under TRAIN, the threshold exemption is taxable income not exceeding ₱250,000 [1].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

Under Section 74(A), every individual subject to income tax under Sections 24 and 25(A) who receives self-employment income — whether it is their sole income or combined with salaries, wages, or other fixed/determinable income — must file a declaration of estimated income for the current taxable year [2]. Self-employment income means earnings from the practice of a profession or conduct of trade/business as a sole proprietor or as a partner in a partnership [2]. The deadline was April 15, but the TRAIN Law moved it to May 15 of the same taxable year [2][4].

Exempt from filing:
- Nonresident Filipino citizens, as to income from outside the Philippines [2]
- Nonresident aliens not engaged in trade or business in the Philippines [2]

"Estimated tax" means the income tax declared in the prior year's final adjusted annual return, minus allowed credits; file an amended declaration if you expect to owe more [3]. Payment is in four installments — at declaration, August 15, November 15, and May 15 of the following year [4].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

Under RR 8-2018, individuals earning purely from self-employment/practice of profession whose gross sales/receipts and other non-operating income do not exceed the VAT threshold (₱3,000,000) may choose either the graduated rates under Sec. 24(A)(2)(a), or an 8% tax on gross sales/receipts and other non-operating income in excess of ₱250,000, in lieu of graduated income tax and the Sec. 116 percentage tax [6][2].

Key conditions:
- You must signify the election in the 1st Quarter Percentage and/or Income Tax Return (or initial quarter return of a new business/profession); otherwise you default to graduated rates. The election is irrevocable for that taxable year [6][2].
- Not available to VAT-registered taxpayers (any amount of sales), those subject to other percentage taxes under Title V (except Sec. 116), or GPP partners on their distributive share [6][2].
- If gross sales/receipts exceed the VAT threshold during the year, you automatically fall under graduated rates, with tax credit for prior quarters' payments [2].
- Financial statements need not be attached to the final return, but bookkeeping and invoicing rules still apply [2][4].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

Walang fixed na piso amount sa konteksto — depende sa iyong **declared monthly earnings** (Monthly Salary Credit).

- Bilang self-employed, ang idineklarang buwanang kita sa SSS registration ang ituturing na monthly compensation, at ikaw ang magbabayad ng employer at employee share [5].
- Ang rate at schedule ay itinatakda ng Social Security Commission [5][2]. Sa schedule na nasa konteksto: 2023–2024 ay 14% (9.5% ER / 4.5% EE) na may MSC range P4,000–P30,000; 2025 ay 15% (10%/5%) na may range P5,000–P35,000 [4].
- Kung ang kita ay mas mababa sa minimum MSC o lampas sa maximum, gamitin ang minimum o maximum MSC [6].
- Remittance: quarterly para sa self-employed [3].

General guidance lamang ito, hindi propesyonal na payo sa buwis.

The premise is incorrect: the 8% income tax rate option is **not** available to a VAT-registered taxpayer, regardless of the amount of gross sales/receipts [1][4]. It is also unavailable to taxpayers subject to other Percentage Taxes under Title V (except Sec. 116) and to GPP partners on their distributive share [1][4].

If you want the 8% option, you would first have to become a non-VAT taxpayer:

- A VAT taxpayer who did not exceed the VAT threshold in the immediately preceding three-year period may opt to be non-VAT and avail of the 8% option, updating registration records on or before the first quarter of the taxable year [2][5].
- You remain liable for VAT until registration is updated and while VAT-registered invoices/receipts are still issued [2][5].
- Then signify the 8% election in the 1st Quarter Percentage and/or Income Tax Return; it is irrevocable for the year [1].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

As a person subject to internal revenue taxes, you must keep and use a relevant and appropriate set of bookkeeping records duly authorized by the Secretary of Finance, showing all transactions and results of operations, from which taxes due can be readily and accurately determined at any time of the year [1].

- If you claim the optional standard deduction, you need not submit financial statements with your return, but you must keep records of your gross sales or gross receipts as required by regulations [5].
- If your gross annual sales, earnings, receipts or output exceed ₱3,000,000, your books must be audited yearly by an independent CPA, with the return accompanied by an Account Information Form [1][7].
- Books and records are open to BIR examination, generally only once per taxable year for income tax purposes, with exceptions such as fraud, requested reinvestigation, or withholding tax verification [4].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

- If sales exceed the VAT threshold during the year, you automatically fall under graduated rates, with tax credit for prior quarterly payments [5].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

Under TRAIN (RR 8-2018), individual taxable income is taxed as follows [1][8]:

**Effective Jan 1, 2023 onwards:**
- Up to ₱250,000 — exempt
- Over ₱250,000 to ₱400,000 — 15% of excess over ₱250,000
- Over ₱400,000 to ₱800,000 — ₱22,500 + 20% of excess over ₱400,000
- Over ₱800,000 to ₱2,000,000 — ₱102,500 + 25% of excess over ₱800,000
- Over ₱2,000,000 to ₱8,000,000 — ₱402,500 + 30% of excess over ₱2,000,000
- Over ₱8,000,000 — ₱2,202,500 + 35% of excess over ₱8,000,000 [1][3]

**Jan 1, 2018–Dec 31, 2022:** same brackets but 20%, 25% (₱30,000 base), 30% (₱130,000), 32% (₱490,000), and 35% (₱2,410,000) [1].

Self-employed individuals/professionals below the ₱3,000,000 VAT threshold may instead opt for the 8% rate on gross sales/receipts in excess of ₱250,000 [3][7]. General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

rows.answer:
Section 116 imposes a tax equivalent to **three percent (3%) of gross quarterly sales or receipts** on any person whose sales or receipts are VAT-exempt (under Sec. 109(z)) and who is not VAT-registered [2]. Returns are filed quarterly, with payment within 25 days after the end of each taxable quarter; if VAT registration is cancelled, the tax accrues from the cancellation date [1]. Anyone retiring from a percentage-tax business must notify the BIR, file and pay within 20 days after closing [1].

When you don't pay it:
- If you opt for the 8% income tax rate (available to self-employed/professionals below the VAT threshold), the 8% is in lieu of the graduated rates *and* Section 116 percentage tax [4][7].
- If you choose graduated rates instead, you continue paying the Section 116 percentage tax [5].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

rows.answer:
Individuals engaged in business or practice of profession, regardless of the amount of sales/receipts, must file Quarterly Income Tax Returns on or before **May 15, August 15, and November 15** for the first, second, and third quarters of the current year, respectively [2]. There is no fourth quarterly return \u2014 instead, the annual Income Tax Return is due not later than the 15th day of the fourth month after the close of the calendar year, i.e., April 15 [2].

A couple of related points:
- If the annual tax due exceeds P2,000, you may pay in two equal installments: the first upon filing the annual return, the second on or before October 15 [2].
- Miss an installment date and the whole unpaid tax becomes due immediately, with penalties reckoned from the original due date [1].

This is general guidance, not professional tax advice.

An individual earning purely compensation income whose taxable income does not exceed Two Hundred Fifty Thousand Pesos (P 250,000.00); b. An individual whose Income Tax has been correctly withheld by his employer, provided that such individual has only one employer for the taxable year; and c. A minimum wage earner. An individual whose sole income has been subjected to Final Withholding Tax is also not required to file Income Tax Return. In all cases, all individuals deriving compensation income, regardless of the amount, from two (2) or more concurrent or successive employers at any time during the taxable year, are not qualified for substituted filing. Thus, they are still required to file a return. Individuals engaged in business/practice of profession, regardless of amount of sales/receipts, are required to file Quarterly Income Tax Return on or before May 15, August 15 and November 15 for the first, second and third quarters of the current year, respectively pursuant to Section 74(A) of the Tax Code, as amended; and to file an annual Income Tax Return not later than the fifteenth (15th) day of the fourth month following the close of the calendar year or April 15 as provided under Section 51(C)(1) of the Tax Code, as amended. When the tax due is in excess of Two Thousand Pesos (P 2,000.00), the individual may elect to pay the tax in two (2) equal installments, wherein the first installment shall be paid at the time the annual Income Tax Return is filed and the second installment paid on or before October 15 following the close of the calendar year.

rows.answer:
A mixed income earner is taxed on both streams, and the treatment of the business side depends on the option chosen:

- **8% option** (available only if gross sales/receipts do not exceed the VAT threshold): total tax due = tax on compensation using the graduated rates, plus 8% applied to total gross sales/receipts and other non-operating income from business, in lieu of the graduated rates and the Section 116 percentage tax [1][7][3].
- **Graduated rates option**: the taxable income from compensation and from business/practice of profession are combined, and the income tax due is computed on the total [1][7][5].

Important: the ₱250,000 deduction allowed for those earning purely from self-employment does NOT apply to mixed income earners under the 8% option, since it is already built into the first tier of the graduated rates; any excess of ₱250,000 over actual taxable compensation is not creditable against business income [2][7][8].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

Yes. A self-employed member is considered both employee and employer at the same time [4][5], and the monthly earnings declared at registration with the SSS are treated as his/her monthly compensation, on which he/she pays **both** the employer and employee contributions [1][3].

Other points that apply:
- The contribution amount follows the monthly salary credits, schedule and rate fixed by the Commission, which also apply to self-employed and voluntary members [1][8].
- Self-employed members remit monthly contributions quarterly on dates the Commission specifies, and payment for one, two or all months of a quarter may be made in the month following that quarter [6].
- Coverage is compulsory for self-employed persons, including self-employed professionals and single proprietors [7].

This is general guidance, not professional tax advice.

Direct contributors are those who have the capacity to pay premiums, namely [2]:

- Those gainfully employed and bound by an employer-employee relationship
- The self-earning
- Professional practitioners
- Migrant workers
- Lifetime members
- Their qualified dependents

Everyone else (and their qualified dependents), including those subsidized under special laws, are indirect contributors whose premiums are subsidized by the national government [1]. Program membership is simplified into just these two types [3]. Direct contributors may receive additional program benefits, and self-employed direct contributors must pay missed contributions with interest of up to 1.5% compounded monthly for self-earning persons, professional practitioners, and migrant workers [3][8]. This is general guidance, not professional tax advice.

Yes. Pag-IBIG coverage is mandatory for a self-employed person, regardless of trade, business or occupation, with an income of at least P1,000 a month and not over 60 years old — including self-employed professionals, single proprietors, business partners, freelancers not under an employer-employee relationship, and informal-sector workers [4]. Key conditions:

- A self-employed person subject to compulsory SSS coverage is treated by the Fund as both employee and employer, so both the employee and employer contributions must be paid [4][2].
- Actual SSS membership is not required; it is enough that the person ought to be compulsorily covered by SSS [4].
- The self-employed subject to compulsory coverage must register with the Fund within 30 days from the date he or she started being self-employed [8].
- One who ceased to be self-employed may continue paying personally as a voluntary member [2].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

Under the Pag-IBIG rules, contributions are based on monthly compensation:

- Employees earning **not more than P1,500/month** – 1% [1][2]
- Employees earning **more than P1,500/month** – 2% [1][2]
- **All employers** – 2% of the monthly compensation of covered employees [1][2]

The maximum monthly compensation used in computing both employee and employer contributions is P5,000, though the Board may adjust this maximum and the rates from time to time [1][2]. The same rates apply to self-employed and voluntary members [1]. A member may contribute more than required, but the employer is only obliged to contribute the required amount unless it agrees to match the increase [1]. Employers cannot deduct or recover their own share from employees' compensation [1][2]. Full-time spouses who volunteer use one-half of the employed spouse's monthly compensation as basis and pay no employer share [1].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

Covered employees and employers shall contribute to the Fund based on the monthly compensation of covered employees as follows: a. Employees earning not more than One thousand five hundred pesos (P1,500.00) per month – one percent (1 %). b. Employees earning more than One thousand five hundred pesos (P1,500.00) per month -two percent (2%). c. All employers – two percent (2%) of the monthly compensation of all covered employees. The maximum monthly compensation to be used in computing employee and employer contributions shall not be more than Five thousand pesos (P5,000.00); Provided, that this maximum and the contribution rates may be fixed from time to time by the Board through rules and regulations adopted by it, taking into consideration actuarial calculations and rates of benefits. Provided further, that the foregoing rates shall likewise be the same for the self-employed and voluntary members. A member may, however, be allowed to contribute more than what is required herein should he or she so desires. The employer, however, shall only be mandated to contribute what is required under these Rules unless the employer agrees to match the member’s increased contribution. Notwithstanding any contract to the contrary, an employer shall not deduct, directly or indirectly, from the compensation of its employees covered by the Fund, or otherwise recover from them, the employer’s contribution with respect to such employees. Section 2. Full-time Spouse. Full-time spouses who volunteer to be covered by the Fund as provided for under these Rules, shall adopt as a basis of monthly contributions one-half (½) of the monthly compensation income of the employed spouse. The full-time spouse shall not be required to pay the employer’s contribution. Section 3. Contributions of Member with Multiple Employers. In cases where a member has two or more employers, such member shall contribute monthly to the Fund a percentage of his or her monthly compensation per employer, which shall be matched by the latter in accordance with Section 1 of this Rule. Persons required to pay internal revenue taxes must keep a journal and a ledger or their equivalents [4][8]. Those whose quarterly sales, earnings, receipts or output do not exceed P50,000 may instead keep a simplified set of bookkeeping records authorized by the Secretary of Finance, showing all transactions and results of operations so taxes can be accurately determined at any time [4][1][8].

Other conditions:
- If gross annual sales/receipts exceed P3,000,000 (as amended by the TRAIN Law), the books must be audited yearly by an independent CPA, with the income tax return accompanied by an Account Information Form [3][6].
- Subsidiary books are optional, but once kept they form part of the accounting system and follow the same rules [1].
- Books must be in a native language, English or Spanish; other languages require a certified translation [1][2].
- Books must be preserved until the last day for BIR assessment under Section 203 [2].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

A 25% surcharge on the amount due applies, in addition to the tax itself, for cases such as failure to file a return and pay the tax due on the prescribed date, filing with the wrong internal revenue officer (unless authorized), failure to pay a deficiency tax within the time in the notice of assessment, or failure to pay the full or part of the tax shown on a return (or tax due where no return is required) by the due date [2].

What changes it:
- If there is **willful neglect** to file within the prescribed period, or a **false or fraudulent return** is willfully made, the penalty is **50%** of the tax or deficiency tax [2].
- On top of the surcharge, unpaid amounts also bear 20% interest per annum from the date prescribed for payment until fully paid [1].

This is general guidance, not professional tax advice.

Under Section 51(A)(1), the following must file an income tax return [3]:

- Every Filipino citizen residing in the Philippines
- Every Filipino citizen residing abroad, on Philippine-source income
- Every alien residing in the Philippines, on Philippine-source income
- Every nonresident alien engaged in trade or business or the exercise of a profession in the Philippines

Exceptions (not required to file): individuals whose taxable income does not exceed P250,000 under Sec. 24(A)(2)(a) [1]; individuals with pure compensation income correctly withheld [3]; those whose sole income was subjected to final withholding tax; and those exempt from income tax under law [6]. However, a Philippine citizen or alien engaged in business or practice of a profession must file regardless of the amount of gross income [1][4], and those with two or more employers during the year must still file [6]. General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

Under Section 74(A), every individual subject to income tax under Sections 24 and 25(A) who receives self-employment income — whether it is the sole income or combined with salaries, wages, or other fixed/determinable income — must file a declaration of estimated income for the current taxable year [2]. Self-employment income means earnings from the practice of a profession or from trade/business as a sole proprietor or as a partner [2]. The deadline, originally April 15, was moved to May 15 by the TRAIN Law [2][4].

- Payment is in four installments: at declaration, August 15, November 15, and the fourth on or before May 15 of the following year with the final adjusted return [4].
- Not required: nonresident Filipino citizens (income from outside the Philippines) and nonresident aliens not engaged in trade or business here [2].

BIR RR 8-2018 restates quarterly filing on May 15, August 15, and November 15 for those in business/profession, regardless of sales [6].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

- Financial statements need not be attached; bookkeeping/invoicing rules still apply [2].

As a person required to pay internal revenue taxes, you must keep and use a relevant and appropriate set of bookkeeping records duly authorized by the Secretary of Finance, showing all transactions and results of operations so that taxes due can be readily and accurately ascertained at any time of the year [1]. If you claim the optional standard deduction, you are not required to submit financial statements with your return, but you must still keep records pertaining to your gross sales or gross receipts as required by rules issued by the Secretary of Finance [5].

Conditions that change this:
- If your gross annual sales/receipts exceed ₱3,000,000, your books must be audited and examined yearly by an independent CPA, with your ITR accompanied by an Account Information Form [1][7].
- Your books are subject to BIR examination, generally only once per taxable year for income tax purposes, with exceptions (e.g. fraud, requested reinvestigation) [4].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

- Not over ₱250,000: exempt

- ₱800,000–₱2,000,000: ₱102,500 + 25%

Section 116 imposes a tax equal to **3% of gross quarterly sales or receipts** on any person whose sales/receipts are VAT-exempt (under Sec. 109(z)) and who is not VAT-registered [2].

Key points:
- It is filed and paid quarterly — a return of gross sales/receipts/earnings, with tax due within 25 days after the end of each taxable quarter [1]. If your VAT registration is cancelled and you become liable under Sec. 116, the tax accrues from the cancellation date [1]. Someone retiring from business must file and pay within 20 days after closing [1].
- You are **not** liable for Sec. 116 tax if you validly elect the 8% income tax rate, since the 8% is in lieu of the graduated rates and the Sec. 116 percentage tax [4][7][6].
- If you opt for graduated rates instead, you continue paying the Sec. 116 percentage tax [5].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

Individuals engaged in business or the practice of a profession — regardless of the amount of sales/receipts — must file Quarterly Income Tax Returns on or before **May 15 (1st quarter), August 15 (2nd quarter), and November 15 (3rd quarter)** of the current year [2]. The annual return is then due not later than the 15th day of the fourth month after the close of the calendar year, i.e. April 15 [2]. If the annual tax due exceeds P2,000, you may elect to pay in two equal installments: the first upon filing the annual return, the second on or before October 15 [2]. Note that missing an installment date makes the whole unpaid tax due, with delinquency penalties reckoned from the original due date [1].

This is general guidance, not professional tax advice.

A mixed income earner (both compensation and business/profession income) is taxed on the two streams as follows:

- **If the 8% option is chosen for business income:** total tax due = (1) tax on taxable compensation using the graduated rates, plus (2) 8% of total gross sales/receipts and other non-operating income from business/profession [1][7]. The 8% is in lieu of the graduated tax and the Section 116 percentage tax on that business income [7]. The ₱250,000 deduction allowed to those earning purely from self-employment is NOT available, since it is already built into the first tier of the graduated rates on compensation; any unused portion is not creditable against business income [2][8].
- **If the graduated rates are chosen:** taxable income from compensation and from business/profession are combined, then taxed under the graduated schedule [1][7][5].
- The 8% option is unavailable if gross sales exceed the VAT threshold [2].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

rows.answer:
Under the Pag-IBIG law and its IRR, contributions are based on the employee's monthly compensation [1][2]:

- Employees earning **not more than P1,500/month** – 1% [1][2]
- Employees earning **more than P1,500/month** – 2% [1][2]
- **All employers** – 2% of the monthly compensation of all covered employees [1][2]

The maximum monthly compensation used to compute both shares is P5,000, though the Board may adjust this maximum and the rates from time to time [1][2]. The same rates apply to self-employed and voluntary members, and a member may opt to contribute more — but the employer is only required to remit the mandated amount unless it agrees to match the increase [1]. Employers cannot deduct or recover their own share from employees' pay [1][2].

This is general guidance, not professional tax advice.

citations.content: RULE VI CONTRIBUTIONS Section 1. Rate of Contributions. Covered employees and employers shall contribute to the Fund based on the monthly compensation of covered employees as follows: a. Employees earning not more than One thousand five hundred pesos (P1,500.00) per month – one percent (1 %). b. Employees earning more than One thousand five hundred pesos (P1,500.00) per month -two percent (2%). c. All employers – two percent (2%) of the monthly compensation of all covered employees. The maximum monthly compensation to be used in computing employee and employer contributions shall not be more than Five thousand pesos (P5,000.00); Provided, that this maximum and the contribution rates may be fixed from time to time by the Board through rules and regulations adopted by it, taking into consideration actuarial calculations and rates of benefits. Provided further, that the foregoing rates shall likewise be the same for the self-employed and voluntary members. A member may, however, be allowed to contribute more than what is required herein should he or she so desires. The employer, however, shall only be mandated to contribute what is required under these Rules unless the employer agrees to match the member’s increased contribution. Notwithstanding any contract to the contrary, an employer shall not deduct, directly or indirectly, from the compensation of its employees covered by the Fund, or otherwise recover from them, the employer’s contribution with respect to such employees. Section 2. Full-time Spouse. Full-time spouses who volunteer to be covered by the Fund as provided for under these Rules, shall adopt as a basis of monthly contributions one-half (½) of the monthly compensation income of the employed spouse. The full-time spouse shall not be required to pay the employer’s contribution. Section 3. Contributions of Member with Multiple Employers. In cases where a member has two or more employers, such member shall contribute monthly to the Fund a percentage of his or her monthly compensation per employer, which shall be matched by the latter in accordance with Section 1 of this Rule. All persons required by law to pay internal revenue taxes — including self-employed individuals — must keep a journal and a ledger or their equivalents [8]. If quarterly sales, earnings, receipts or output do not exceed ₱50,000, a simplified set of bookkeeping records authorized by the Secretary of Finance may be used instead, showing all transactions and results of operations so taxes can be accurately determined at any time [4][1].

Other conditions:
- **Audit requirement:** under the TRAIN Law, if gross *annual* sales/receipts exceed ₱3,000,000, books must be audited yearly by an independent CPA and the return accompanied by an Account Information Form [3][6].
- **Subsidiary books** are optional but, if kept, form part of the accounting system and follow the same rules [1].
- Books must be in a native language, English or Spanish [1], and preserved until the last day of the assessment period under Section 203 [2].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

A 25% surcharge (civil penalty) on the amount due applies, in addition to the tax itself, for:

- Filing with an internal revenue officer other than the one required, unless authorized by the Commissioner [2]
- Failure to pay a deficiency tax within the time stated in the notice of assessment [2]
- Failure to pay the full or part of the tax shown on a return, or the full tax due where no return is required, on or before the due date [2]

The surcharge rises to 50% for willful neglect to file within the prescribed period or for a willfully false or fraudulent return [2]. Unpaid amounts also earn 20% interest per annum from the date prescribed for payment until fully paid [1].

This is general guidance, not professional tax advice.

- The estimated tax is paid in four installments: at declaration, August 15, November 15, and the final one with the annual return (now May 15) [4].

CHAPTER XII – QUARTERLY CORPORATE INCOME TAX ANNUAL DECLARATION AND QUARTERLY PAYMENTS OF INCOME TAXES Section 74. Declaration of Income Tax for Individuals. – (A) In General. – Except as otherwise provided in this Section, every individual subject to income tax under Sections 24 and 25(A) of this Title, who is receiving self-employment income, whether it constitutes the sole source of his income or in combination with salaries, wages and other fixed or determinable income, shall make and file a declaration of his estimated income for the current taxable year on or before April 15 of the same taxable year. In general, self-employment income consists of the earnings derived by the individual from the practice of profession or conduct of trade or business carried on by him as a sole proprietor or by a partnership of which he is a member. Nonresident Filipino citizens, with respect to income from without the Philippines, and nonresident aliens not engaged in trade or business in the Philippines, are not required to render a declaration of estimated income tax. - Contribution rate: 15% sa 2025 (10% employer share + 5% employee share) [4]
- Minimum MSC: P5,000; maximum MSC: P35,000 sa 2025 [4]
- Kung ang kita ay mas mababa sa minimum MSC o mas mataas sa maximum, ang contribution ay base sa minimum o maximum MSC [6]
- Bahagi na tumutumbas sa MSC na lampas P20,000 ay napupunta sa mandatory Provident Fund [4]

Remittance: quarterly ang bayad ng self-employed, at ang buwang bahagi ay maaaring bayaran sa buwan kasunod ng quarter [3].

General guidance lang ito, hindi professional tax advice.

Correction: the 8% option is **not** available to a VAT-registered taxpayer, regardless of the amount of gross sales/receipts, nor to taxpayers subject to other percentage taxes (except Sec. 116) or to GPP partners on their distributive share [1][4].

To get there and elect it:

- If you did not exceed the VAT threshold within the immediately preceding 3-year period, you may opt to become a non-VAT taxpayer and avail of the 8% rate; update your registration records on or before the first quarter of the taxable year. You stay liable for VAT while registration is not updated and VAT invoices/receipts are still issued [2][5].
- As an existing non-VAT taxpayer, file BIR Form 1905 to end-date the Percentage Tax type, and signify the intention to elect 8% in the 1st Quarter Percentage and/or Income Tax Return (or initial quarter return for a new business) — otherwise graduated rates apply, and the election is irrevocable for the year [1][6].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.

rows.answer:
You must keep a relevant and appropriate set of bookkeeping records duly authorized by the Secretary of Finance, showing all transactions and results of operations, from which taxes due can be readily and accurately determined at any time of the year [1].

Other conditions:
- If your gross annual sales, earnings, receipts or output exceed ₱3,000,000, your books must be audited and examined yearly by an independent CPA, and your ITR must be accompanied by an Account Information Form (AIF) [1][7].
- If you claim the optional standard deduction, you need not attach financial statements, but you must still keep records of your gross sales or gross receipts as required by regulations [5].
- Your books are subject to BIR examination (generally once per taxable year for income tax, with exceptions like fraud or reinvestigation requests), and if you retire from business you must submit them within 10 days [4].

General guidance only, not professional tax advice.
